notes.meaning: The count now reaches the tribe of Asher. A 'clan' here means a large group descended from one of Asher's sons or grandsons, named in his honor, not one household. The list matches the sons of Asher given in Genesis 46 and 1 Chronicles 7. One son, Ishvah, is left out because no clan came from him.
In a long list of men, one daughter of Asher is named: Serah. Her name stands in the family record of Asher alongside the clans of her brothers.
Asher now has 53,400 fighting men. That is 11,900 more than at the first count at Mount Sinai, nearly forty years before. It was one of the tribes that grew during the desert years.

Next comes Naphtali, with four clans. They match the sons of Naphtali named in Genesis 46. Naphtali now has 45,400 men, which is 8,000 fewer than at the first count. Some tribes grew in the desert, and some shrank.

The full count is 601,730 men, only 1,820 fewer than at Mount Sinai. A whole generation had died in the desert, yet God raised up almost the same number in their place. This shows His justice in judging sin, His mercy in giving a new generation, and His faithfulness in keeping His promise to Abraham's family.

God tells Moses how the land of Canaan will be shared out. An 'inheritance' is land that belongs to a family and is handed down. Bigger tribes get more land, and smaller tribes get less, which is a simple and fair rule. God says 'to these,' the people just counted, so the promise would come true for them, not someday for others. Moses himself would not enter the land, so this direction was really for Joshua, who came after him.

The land was also to be shared out by 'lot,' a kind of drawing that left the choice to God. Older teachers explain that the lot decided where each tribe would live, while the size of its land followed the rule of bigger and smaller tribes. The lot was not luck, for 'the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD' (Proverbs 16:33). So each tribe could take its land with thanks, as a gift chosen by God. Some also see here a picture of believers' share in heaven, given by God's kindness (Colossians 1:12).

The tribe of Levi is counted on its own, because God had set it apart to serve Him. Its three main branches came from Levi's sons Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. The list of smaller clans stops after five names, so the story can turn to the family of Moses and Aaron. They came from Kohath through his son Amram.

Moses and Aaron's mother, Jochebed, is named, which is unusual in Bible family lists. Some older Bible teachers say 'daughter of Levi' means a woman from Levi's tribe who lived long after Levi himself. Others take it word for word. If so, Moses honestly recorded a marriage that God's law would later forbid, which made God's kindness to his family shine even more.

Aaron had four sons, but Nadab and Abihu died when they offered 'unauthorized fire,' worship God had not asked for (Leviticus 10). With two sons gone, the priesthood rested on just two men, yet God kept it going. Their death is told again as a warning, especially to priests, to serve God with care and not carelessly.

The Levites number 23,000 males a month old and up, only 1,000 more than before. They were not counted with the other tribes because this count was for taking and sharing the land. The Levites would not get a region of their own, because they belonged to God's service.

This count was made by Moses and Eleazar the priest, on the plains of Moab by the Jordan River, across from Jericho. The first count had been made with Aaron, who had since died. The change of names points ahead to how much had changed in the people.

Not one man from the first count was still alive except Caleb and Joshua. God had said the grumbling generation would die in the desert (Numbers 14:29), and He did just what He said. Many of them were young enough to have lived longer, so it was God's judgment, not just old age. He also kept His promise to spare Caleb and Joshua, who had trusted Him. The Levites were not under this sentence, since they were not in that count. The passage calls us to take sin seriously, turn back to God, and treasure the salvation Christ gives.
